sections.body_en:
A person to whom a firstborn son is born must redeem him after thirty days, by giving the kohen the value of five shekels by the sacred shekel, as it is said (Shemot 13:2): "Sanctify to Me every firstborn, whatever opens the womb among the children of Israel, of man and of beast; it is Mine." And it is said (there 13:13): "And every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem." And it is said (Bamidbar 18:16): "And those to be redeemed of them, from a month old you shall redeem, according to your valuation, five shekels of silver by the sacred shekel, which is twenty gera."

In order to understand the reason for the mitzva of the redemption of the firstborn, one must first say that in everything that is first and primal, the hand of Hashem is revealed more. Admittedly, one who lifts his eyes to see and to ask who created these understands that everything is from Hashem; but the routine in which we see the world again and again in all its outward appearances makes us forget the primal questions, such as: where did everything begin, and how does everything live. But when a person meets for the first time something new, just now created, such as a baby for example, his heart is stirred, and he draws closer to faith. And so the Maharal of Prague explains (Gevurot Hashem ch. 38) that everything first resembles in some measure the Creator, blessed be He, who is 'the beginning of existence', and therefore there is holiness in firstborns. There is holiness in the first fruits that grow anew each year on the tree, and we must fulfil with them the mitzva of 'bikkurim' and bring them up to Jerusalem to the kohanim. Likewise there is holiness in the first son who is born, so much so that he cannot live ordinary profane life in this world without our redeeming him as the Torah commands.

Another important aspect should be emphasised in the reason for the mitzva of the redemption of the firstborn. Precisely the holiness and the special virtue revealed in the firstborn son may create a complication both for the parents and for their son. The parents may become excessively proud of their firstborn son, to the point that they think as if they themselves created their son, and forget that they are messengers and partners in bringing their son's soul down into the world. In addition, parents tend to hang great and exaggerated hopes on their firstborn son, something that may foster in him negative traits such as pride, a tendency to selfishness and an exaggerated fear of failure. Against this pride of the parents, which is afterwards projected onto their son, the Torah comes and obligates the father to redeem his son. To emphasise: do not think that this son is your creation and is yours. In truth he is holy and belongs to Hashem, and in order that he may live a profane life in this world, you must redeem him.

There is a great privilege for a father who merits the mitzva of the redemption of the firstborn, because it is a rare mitzva that does not come to every person. First, because anyone to whom a daughter was born first is exempt from the redemption of the firstborn, for only a firstborn son must be redeemed and not a daughter.

Also kohanim and levi'im, or even Israelites who married the daughter of a kohen or the daughter of a levi, are exempt from redeeming their firstborn son (as explained below in halakha 9).

And likewise when the first pregnancy ended in a miscarriage, the son born after it will be exempt from the redemption of the firstborn. And likewise if the firstborn son was born by Caesarean section, he is not redeemed. It turns out, then, that fewer than a third of all parents merit to fulfil the mitzva of the redemption of the firstborn. And since it is a rare mitzva, one tries to fulfil it with beautification: many guests are invited, and a large meal is held, with meat and delicacies.

The redemption of the firstborn son must be with five shekels by the sacred shekel, as it is said (Bamidbar 18:16): "And those to be redeemed of them, from a month old you shall redeem, according to your valuation, five shekels of silver by the sacred shekel, which is twenty gera." The weight of the pure silver that was in five shekels in the time of the Torah is about 85 grams of pure silver. And some say (Kenesset Ha-Gedola, Baḥ and others) that since there is a concern that some error may have crept into the calculation, many are accustomed to be stringent and to reckon the five shekels as a hundred grams of pure silver.

And although it is said in the Torah that in order to redeem the firstborn one must give the kohen five shekels by the sacred shekel, according to the law one need not give the kohen specifically money; one may also give him something of monetary value, the main thing being that the value of what one gives the kohen be the value of five shekels of the time of the Torah. And as we explained, the weight of each shekel was close to twenty grams of pure silver. If so, in practice one can give the kohen actual pure silver weighing a hundred grams, or something whose value equals a hundred grams of silver, such as candlesticks, silver cups, or even fruit and clothes and the like of this value. And everything of course depends on the price of silver on that day (Bekhorot 49b; SA YD 305:3).1

Although one may redeem the firstborn with something of monetary value, with three things one cannot redeem the firstborn, and these are: land, slaves and documents (SA YD 305:3). For the thing with which the firstborn is redeemed must be similar to money, that is, it must be movable and have monetary value in itself. If so, land, which cannot be moved, is excluded from this rule, and likewise documents, which are not themselves money but express a monetary agreement between two people (Bekhorot 51a). Therefore one should not redeem with a cheque, because it is considered a document; that is, the cheque expresses an obligation of the bank account holder towards the recipient of the cheque, that when he comes to the bank he will receive from his account the sum written on the cheque.

Regarding the banknotes of our time, the poskim disagree. Some say that their law is as a promissory note of the state, and since they are not themselves money, one may not redeem with them (Teshuva Me-Ahava vol. 2, 404, and others). And some say that since the state has defined them as actual money, their law is as money and they are fit for redemption (Ḥesed Le-Avraham, first edition, YD 95). As halakha it has been ruled that one should not redeem the firstborn with banknotes (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 305:18).

notes_en.en: The sacred shekel in the language of the Torah is the sela in the language of the Sages. The SA YD 305:1 wrote, following the Rambam, that five shekels are 30 dirhams. R. Ḥaim Na'eh (Shiurei Torah p. 82) calculated according to the Turkish dirham, which is about 3.2 grams, and so five shekels are 96 grams; and many follow this, and some round up to a hundred grams (Yeḥaveh Da'at 4:54). However, it has become clear that the Turks raised its weight by more than ten percent, but for hundreds of years, including in the time of the Rambam, the dirham weighed only 2.83 grams, and so five shekels are 85 grams. And all this is according to the view of the Geonim and the Rambam, that a shekel is 17 grams. But according to Rashi, by the coins that have been found it is 14.2, and so five sela'im are 71 grams (Middot Ve-Shiurei Torah by Rav Benish 31:2; 22:4-6). Since one may redeem with the value of five silver shekels, one must keep up to date with the price of silver. Over the last decades the price of silver has fluctuated extremely. In most years the price of an ounce (about 31 grams) was about five dollars, and at times it rose to fifty dollars. In recent years (5770-5771) its price on the exchange has moved between 15 and 50 dollars. Accordingly it turns out that the price of 85 grams moves between 150 and 500 shekels. And in shops its price is about ten percent higher. The government coins company cast coins weighing 20 grams each for the redemption of the firstborn, but the price it charges for them – about 2,000 shekels and more – is at least four times higher than the price of pure silver of that weight. In practice, one should estimate the value of 85 grams of silver on that day according to its price in a shop, and to remove doubt it is good to calculate a hundred grams.

sections.title_en: 3. The Order of the Redemption and Its Meaning
sections.body_en:
This is the order of the redemption of the firstborn: after the meal has begun, the father gives his firstborn son to the kohen, and the kohen turns to the father with the question: Which do you want more, your firstborn son or the five sela'im (as the sacred shekels were called in the days of the Sages) that you are obligated to give in order to redeem him? And the father answers: I want my firstborn son more. After that the father recites two blessings: a) "Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the redemption of the son." b) "Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who has kept us alive, sustained us and brought us to this time." And immediately afterwards he says to the kohen: "Here are the five sela'im that I am obligated in," and gives the kohen the redemption money. Afterwards the kohen takes a cup of wine and recites "who creates the fruit of the vine" and drinks it. Some are accustomed that the kohen takes myrtle and recites over it "who creates fragrant trees" and smells it (the Sephardi custom), and some were not accustomed to take myrtle (the Ashkenazi custom). After that the kohen blesses the son with the Priestly Blessing and returns him to the father (Tur, following the custom of the Geonim).

Many have asked: what is the meaning of the kohen's question to the father – which do you want more, your son or the five sela'im – and where do we find that the choice is in the father's hands to decide? For it is settled halakha that even if the father does not want to redeem his son, and wants to leave him in the hands of the kohen, he is not permitted to, because even before the redemption the son does not belong to the kohen. The author of the 'Arukh Ha-Shulḥan' explained (YD 305:36) that were it not for the redemption, the firstborn son would have had to be designated only for matters of holiness, because when the firstborn of Israel were saved from the plague of the firstborn in Egypt, they were designated for the service of Hashem, to the point that they would be forbidden to do anything not of holiness. And this is what the kohen asks the father of the son: what do you prefer more – your firstborn son, so that he can conduct himself like all people who engage in their work, and you will redeem him with five sela'im; or do you prefer the five sela'im, and the son will be designated only for matters of holiness? And of course every father prefers to redeem his son so that he can conduct himself like all people.

Two main laws were said regarding a firstborn: one – that he must be redeemed from the kohen, and the second – that he inherits a double portion from his brothers. However, there is a difference in the definition of the firstborn between the two laws. And there are children who are considered firstborn regarding one law and not firstborn regarding the second law, because the firstborn regarding redemption depends on his mother, whereas the firstborn regarding inheritance depends on his father.

For example: a man who has children from his first wife, and married again a woman who has not yet given birth – the first son born to him from his second wife will be obligated in the redemption of the firstborn, for the Torah's definition regarding the redemption of the firstborn is: 'that which opens the womb', that is, the first who comes out of his mother's womb. But regarding inheritance he will not be considered firstborn, because his father already has older sons from his first wife, and the father's inheritance goes according to the father.

On the other hand, if the first pregnancy reached the stage at which the limbs of the foetus had already developed, and after that a miscarriage occurred, and afterwards the mother conceives again and gives birth to a male son, he will not be considered firstborn regarding the redemption of the firstborn, because he is not 'that which opens the womb', for the stillborn was the one that came out first from his mother's womb. But regarding the father's inheritance, even a son born after a miscarriage is considered firstborn to his father, and according to Torah law he inherits a double portion. For it is said in the Torah regarding the law of inheritance (Devarim 21:17): "For he is the first of his strength; the right of the firstborn is his." And the Sages learned from this that one who is firstborn from the father's standpoint, that is, whose father's heart pains him especially when he dies, has the law of inheritance (Mishna Bekhorot 8:1).

A firstborn born by Caesarean section is not redeemed with the redemption of the firstborn, because he was not born in the way of other newborns, and the Torah said: "that which opens the womb", that is, the one who opens the womb, meaning the firstborn who came out of the natural opening of his mother's womb, and not one who came out by Caesarean section (SA YD 305:24).2

notes_en.en: When the mother had difficulty in her labour, and they drew out the foetus with a vacuum pump, the firstborn is obligated in redemption, for he came out through the opening of the womb. And likewise when they needed to draw out the foetus with forceps, since he came out through the opening of the womb, he is obligated in redemption. And likewise when the mother had difficulty in her labour and the doctors needed to widen the opening of the womb with scissors so that the foetus could come out, he is considered to have come out of the opening of the womb and is obligated in redemption (Har Tzvi YD 248; Igrot Moshe YD 3:125).

sections.body_en:
Sometimes a firstborn male son is born to a family, and all the relatives and friends expect that soon they will be invited to the meal of the redemption of the firstborn, but a month passes and the invitation does not arrive. The reason for this is that there was a miscarriage before, and if so the son born afterwards is not (Bamidbar 3:12) "that which opens the womb", that is, he is not the firstborn who opened his mother's womb.

However, if the miscarriage happened before the formation of limbs had begun in the stillborn, the one born after it is obligated in the redemption of the firstborn. For only if the limbs of the stillborn had begun to develop does its coming out open its mother's womb, so that the one born after it is exempt from the redemption of the firstborn; but if its limbs had not formed, there is no opening of the womb in its coming out. In practice, if the miscarriage was up to the fortieth day of conception, the one born after it is obligated in the redemption of the firstborn (SA 305:23). And this is also the agreement of the doctors, that until the fortieth day it is clear that no formation of limbs has yet taken place in the foetus. And if the miscarriage happened after that, if it is clear that the limbs of the foetus had begun to form, the one born after it is exempt from redemption. And when there is a doubt, the one born after it should be redeemed without a blessing. And it is right that a woman who miscarried her first foetus after the fortieth day should clarify well with the doctor what the state of the foetus was, for it is possible that although more than forty days had passed over the foetus, its development stopped before then, and it did not reach a level of development of more than forty days, and consequently no formation at all took place in it, neither of limbs nor of flesh; and then according to all views they will need to redeem the one born after it. One should also note that the calculation accepted today in clinics also includes two weeks before the beginning of the pregnancy, whereas the calculation that determines the halakha begins from the day of fertilisation, which is the day of ovulation or the day after it.3

notes_en.en:
In a normal pregnancy, forty-two days after ovulation there is certainly formation of limbs, and after forty days there is a doubt whether the formation of limbs has begun. It is important to note that in clinics it is accepted to calculate the pregnancy from the time of the last period, but fertilisation actually takes place at least 14 days after that. And for the calculation, one should calculate the age of the foetus from the time of fertilisation, which takes place on the day of ovulation or the day after it.
The Rema wrote, following the Mahari"k (YD 305:23): "As long as the limbs of the stillborn are not formed, it does not exempt the one who comes after it, and even in our time we rely on this." And in the view of the Ḥakham Tzvi (104) and the Shevut Yaakov (vol. 1, 9), even if the limbs of the stillborn had not begun to form but there were in it a kind of thin sinews like flesh, one need not redeem the one who comes after it. In any case, if no more than forty days had passed over the foetus, it is clear that the one who comes after it needs redemption.

sections.body_en:
It is said in the Torah (Bamidbar 18:16): "And those to be redeemed of them, from a month old you shall redeem," that is, the redemption must be held after the firstborn has completed a month of days. And since an unspecified month is thirty days, after thirty days have passed over the firstborn and he reaches his thirty-first day, it is a mitzva to redeem him. If they redeemed the firstborn before that, they have not fulfilled with him the mitzva of the redemption of the firstborn. On the other hand, once he has reached his thirty-first day, he should be redeemed immediately, and the redemption should not be postponed to another day. In counting the days, both the day of birth and the day of the redemption are included. It turns out that the redemption will always be four weeks and two days after the birth. For example, if the son was born on Sunday, the redemption will be held on Tuesday. And if he was born on Monday, the redemption will be held on Wednesday.

Some of the poskim said that the main calculation depends on the exact time of the lunar month, which is twenty-nine days and another twelve hours and about forty-four minutes (793 parts of an hour that has 1,080 parts). That is, if the son was born at the beginning of the day, according to their view one could hold the redemption already on the thirtieth day; and if the son was born at the end of the day, one could not redeem the son on the night of the thirty-first day but only in its middle (Baḥ and Shakh).

In practice it is fitting to take this view into account too, and beyond being careful not to redeem before the thirty-first day, to pay attention that from the time of birth until the time of the redemption more than twenty-nine full days and another half a day and forty-four minutes will have passed (Pitḥei Teshuva YD 305:17; Da'at Kohen 185).

If the firstborn's father did not redeem on that day, it is a mitzva for him to hasten to redeem him as soon as possible. And if the father did not redeem his son, it is a mitzva for the son when he grows up to redeem himself; and as long as he is alive, the moment he hears that he was not redeemed, it is a mitzva for him to hasten to redeem himself.

sections.title_en: 7. The Meal of Mitzva and Redemption at Night
sections.body_en:
There is a mitzva to hold a meal at the time of the redemption of the son. And it is customary first to wash the hands, to break bread and eat a little of it, and afterwards to perform the redemption. The book 'Terumat Ha-Deshen' wrote that the reason for holding the meal is to publicise the act of redemption to the many. And one may add that at this meal we publicise and recall the kindness that Hashem did with us when He took us out of Egypt, and killed their firstborn and saved our firstborn. And there is in this mitzva also an expression of the special holiness that is in Israel, that every firstborn is naturally holy, and in order that he may engage also in profane matters, he must be redeemed.

This meal is called a se'udat mitzva. Therefore even when its time falls in 'the Nine Days' of the month of Av, when it is customary not to eat meat and not to drink wine because of the mourning over the destruction of the Temple, meat and wine are served at the meal (Rema 551:10). There is great virtue in taking part in the meal of the redemption of the son, and some say that whoever eats of it is considered as if he fasted 84 fasts (Sedei Ḥemed, Ma'arekhet Samekh, 54).

According to the law, one may perform the redemption of the firstborn on the night of the thirty-first or on its day. But some wrote that the custom is to hold the redemption specifically by day (Shakh YD 305:12), and gave several halakhic reasons for this (that in this way the redemption will always be held after twenty-nine and a half days and forty-four minutes, as explained in the previous halakha). And some wrote that even by custom one may hold the redemption at night (Ginat Veradim YD, rule 6, 10; Sedei Ḥemed, Ma'arekhet Peh, rule 39). And so is the practice: whenever there is a need for it, the redemption and the meal are held at night.

sections.title_en: 8. Should the Kohen Return the Money?
sections.body_en:
It is told in the Talmud (Bekhorot 51b) about Rabbi Tarfon, who was a kohen, that when they would give him the money of the redemption of the firstborn, he was accustomed to return it after some time. Apparently he did so mainly towards poor parents (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan YD 305:30). And so too Rabbi Ḥanina the kohen was accustomed: he would return the redemption money to the father of the son. But when once the father of the son began to walk around near him, to hint to him that he should already return the redemption money, Rabbi Ḥanina rebuked him and said: You are not acting well, and it is even possible that you have not fulfilled the obligation of the redemption of the firstborn; for if you are certain that you will receive the money back, it is a sign that you did not give it wholeheartedly, and you did not fulfil the mitzva. And so it was ruled in the 'Shulḥan Arukh' (YD 305:8) that the kohen may return the money to the father of the son, but on condition that he does not always return it. For if he always returns it, all the parents will come to him, and through this the other kohanim will lose out.

One of the reasons for the custom of kohanim to return the redemption money is that these gifts were meant to support the kohanim while they fulfil their sanctified role; and now that the Temple is destroyed and they do not fulfil their role, the kohanim preferred to return the precious gift. But since according to the law the obligation remains in its place, the kohanim should be careful at times not to return the money, so that the mitzva is not forgotten.

One of the later poskim, the author of 'She'elat Yaavetz' (vol. 1, 155), wanted to innovate that only in the past, when the kohanim had their lineage established by a beit din, were they entitled by law to receive the redemption money, and it was regarding them that the halakha was said that they may not always return the redemption money to the parents. But today, when the kohanim's lineage is established only by presumption and tradition, kohanim may always return the redemption money. And if they do not return it, they enter a concern of theft, because there is no complete certainty that they are indeed kohanim. He further added that it is worthwhile to redeem the son with several kohanim, so as to be sure that one of them is truly a kohen.

But the other Aḥaronim did not accept his words (Ḥatam Sofer, end of siman 291). And the 'Arukh Ha-Shulḥan' even came out sharply against his view, and wrote that it is forbidden to say so, because it diminishes the virtue of the kehuna. And further, that presumption is a great foundation that one can rely on, and Heaven forbid to make of it even a double doubt. Therefore even today a kohen may not regularly return the whole sum of the redemption to the parents, so as not to deprive the other kohanim, and in order to emphasise that the giving of the redemption is a complete giving, and only the kohen may decide whether to give back the redemption money as a gift to the parents of the firstborn.

sections.title_en: 9. The Meaning of the Kehuna, and a Firstborn Born to the Daughter of a Kohen or Levi
sections.body_en:
Originally the firstborns were meant to be the kohanim. And there is a great idea in this, for in this way in every family there would be a person designated for matters of holiness, and so the whole people, with all its families, would be bound to the service of Hashem and to matters of the spirit, since every family would have a representative who would serve in the Temple. But after the firstborns too took part in the sin of the golden calf, they fell from their level, and in their place the tribe of Levi, which did not take part in the sin, was chosen and sanctified. One may learn from this that apparently the idea of the firstborn is still too lofty for us, and there is a concern that instead of the firstborn-kohanim influencing the public as a whole, the public atmosphere and the profane life of the broad public would influence them and cancel their spiritual uniqueness. And in order to educate kohanim who will truly be people of the spirit, one must create a cohesive society that is wholly occupied with matters of holiness. Therefore, after the firstborns sinned in the sin of the golden calf, the tribe of Levi, which did not take part in the sin, was chosen for this.

At that time, after the sin of the golden calf, when the levi'im replaced the firstborns of Israel, the count of the firstborns in Israel came to twenty-two thousand two hundred and seventy-three, whereas the levi'im then numbered only twenty-two thousand. It turns out that two hundred and seventy-three firstborns had to redeem themselves with five shekels, for no levi'im were found in their stead (Bamidbar ch. 3).

And since then, every firstborn born to a kohen or to a levi is exempt from redemption; for if they themselves could be in place of the firstborns of Israel, certainly there is no need for them to redeem themselves. However, an Israelite firstborn is redeemed only with a kohen and not with a levi, for so the Torah commanded, that only a kohen can receive the redemption money.

Also when the father of the firstborn is an Israelite, if his wife is the daughter of a kohen or the daughter of a levi, he need not be redeemed. For the main factor in the firstborn status depends on the mother, as it is said (Shemot 13:2): "whatever opens every womb among the children of Israel"; thus the verse made the obligation depend on the opening of the womb of an Israelite woman, and the daughter of a kohen or the daughter of a levi is not an Israelite woman (Bekhorot 47a; SA YD 305:18). However, the daughter of the daughter of a kohen or the daughter of the daughter of a levi, whose father is an Israelite, are already considered Israelite women, and the firstborn son born to them will be obligated in redemption. So it turns out that sometimes the great-grandfather kohen can be the kohen who redeems his great-grandson, who is the grandson of his daughter and the son of his granddaughter, who married Israelites.

sections.title_en: 10. The Redemption of the Firstborn When There Is No Father
sections.body_en:
When there is no father, for example when he died before the birth of his son, the question arises how the son will be redeemed. This question also exists in the case of a pregnant gentile woman who converts during her first pregnancy and gives birth to her firstborn son after the conversion, when she is already Jewish. For then, although the father of her son is a gentile and at the beginning of the pregnancy the mother too was still a gentile, the son is obligated in redemption. The mother of the firstborn cannot redeem her son, because the mitzva belongs to males. And the question is whether the beit din or the rabbi can fill the father's place and redeem the son, or whether it is preferable to wait until the son grows up and redeems himself.

The Rema and the Taz (YD 305:10) ruled that apart from the father, no one may redeem the son; and therefore one should hang a chain on the little child's neck on which is written that he is a firstborn who has not been redeemed, and when he reaches the age of bar mitzva he will redeem himself. But most poskim wrote that it is preferable that the beit din or the rabbi serve as agents of the newborn child and redeem him from the kohen; for if they wait until the firstborn grows up, there is a concern that he will forget to redeem himself. And further, that ideally it is good to redeem the son at the time set by the Torah, that is, after thirty days. And in their view, when the firstborn is redeemed in place of the father, one even recites "concerning the redemption of the firstborn" (Shakh; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 305:13-14; Igrot Moshe YD 1:195).

And some say that since the matter is disputed, it is preferable that the beit din redeem the firstborn when he is thirty-one days old without a blessing, and when the firstborn reaches the age of thirteen he should redeem himself again out of doubt without a blessing (Ḥatam Sofer 195; Tzitz Eliezer vol. 1, 28:7).
